query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A high‐throughput, multiscale simulation framework that integrates ab initio molecular dynamics with statistical learning of local lattice distortions and short‐range order can be used to accurately predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and volume change at melting in high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase high-entropy alloys (e.g., NiFeCoCr-based or Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni alloys) synthesized under ambient conditions with predominantly FCC structures.
generation.intervention: Perform high-throughput ab initio and Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations across targeted HEA compositions to quantify local lattice distortions and short-range ordering, then train regression models (machine learning algorithms) to map these structural mediators to melting and fusion properties.
generation.conditions: Simulations and subsequent experimental validations are carried out at ambient pressure across a broad compositional landscape of high-entropy alloys with controlled phase homogeneity (limiting secondary phases) and using calibrated simulation conditions with available experimental benchmarks.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order metrics determined from atomic-scale simulations.
generation.mechanism: Atomic-scale structural mediators (local bond length distributions and distortions) influence the free energy landscape, thereby modulating the thermodynamic parameters associated with melting. Statistical models can capture these correlations to yield accurate predictions of melting temperature and fusion thermodynamic properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The integrated simulation-regression approach is expected to predict melting temperature, enthalpy/entropy of fusion, and melting volume changes within approximately ±10% of experimentally measured values, offering improved efficiency and accuracy relative to traditional empirical or experimental methods.
generation.baseline: Traditional experimental characterization methods and simple empirical models yield larger uncertainties and are less efficient for exploring the wide compositional space of high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: The predictive accuracy is expected to hold for single-phase, FCC-based high-entropy alloys. Accuracy may decline for systems exhibiting significant secondary phase formation or non-equilibrium phases, as well as compositions far outside the calibration range of the method.
generation.uncertainty: While correlations between local lattice distortion and macro-scale thermodynamic properties have been suggested by prior work, uncertainties remain in extrapolating these relationships across the full HEA compositional space, particularly for alloys that may exhibit complex phase behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a set of high entropy alloys spanning a broad range of compositions within the targeted family. Measure their melting temperatures, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting using differential scanning calorimetry and dilatometry. Perform parallel high-throughput ab initio molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations to extract local lattice distortion data and short-range order metrics. Train the regression model and compare its predictions against the experimental results.
measurements: Fusion enthalpy and entropy measured by calorimetry methods
Volume change at melting determined via dilatometry
Local structural metrics (lattice distortions, bond length distributions) from X-ray diffraction and EXAFS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predictions of the melting and fusion properties deviate by more than ±10% from experimental measurements for a significant number of tested alloys, or if no statistically significant correlation is found between the computed structural mediators and the measured thermodynamic properties, the hypothesis is falsified.

How Atomic Bonding Plays the Hardness Behavior in the Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni High Entropy Family

Abstract: AbstractA systematic study on a face‐centered cubic‐based compositionally complex alloy system Al–Co–Cr–Cu–Fe–Ni in its single‐phase state is carried out, where a mother senary compound Al8Co17Cr17Cu8Fe17Ni33 and five of its suballoys, obtained by removing one element at a time, are investigated and exhaustively analyzed determining the contribution of each alloying element in the solid solution. The senary and the quinaries are compared using experimental techniques including X‐ray absorption spectroscopy, X‐ray diffraction, transmission electron microscopy, and first principles hybrid Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics simulations. Chemical short‐range order and bond length distances have been determined both at the experimental and computational level. Electronic structure and local atomic distortions up to 5.2 Å have been correlated to the microhardness values. Tunable magnetocaloric effect in transition metal alloys

Abstract: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives.
